extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York; delegates and readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Argues principles and textual interpretations governing the distribution of impeachment, appointment, treaty, and presidential-election powers between the Executive, the Senate, and the House of Representatives under the proposed U.S. Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of accusation and judgment in impeachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign accusing to one branch of the legislature and judging to the other (House originates impeachments; Senate tries them) to avoid making the same persons both accusers and judges and to guard against persecution from a factious spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division avoids the inconvenience and danger of persecution that would arise if the same body both accused and judged. It preserves impartiality by preventing the combination of prosecutorial and adjudicative roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermajority requirement for conviction in impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: A concurrence of two thirds of the Senate is required for conviction in impeachment cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-thirds requirement provides an additional security to innocence, making wrongful conviction less likely and offering as complete a protection to the innocent as can be desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a fit tribunal for impeachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate, given its composition, tenure, and selection method, is a proper receptacle for the power of trying impeachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples and reasons of the thing indicate the Senate is well suited; concerns about undue senatorial influence should be examined power-by-power rather than by vague aggregate fears about aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterbalances to senatorial power residing in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain exclusive powers of the House serve as important counterpoises to authorities conferred on the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These counterweights include the exclusive privilege of originating money bills, the sole right of instituting impeachments, and the House's role in deciding contingent presidential elections — powers that may, in practice, outweigh peculiar attributes of the Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's appointment role is advice-and-consent (ratify or reject)
rubrics_metrics.description: In appointments the President nominates and, with the Senate's advice and consent, appoints; the Senate cannot itself choose appointments but may only ratify or reject the President's nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Senate cannot directly make choices, it is less likely to exhibit favoritism toward appointees: senators may defeat a nomination and force another, but cannot ensure a subsequent nominee will be their preferred candidate; this structure reduces the plausibility of a corrupt bias in impeachment judgments rooted in appointment favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual/contextual interpretation of appointment and recess-appointment clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Clauses about nomination/appointment and recess appointments must be read in connection; the recess-appointment provision supplements the general appointment clause and applies to officers whose appointments are not otherwise provided for in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation should consider (1) the relation of the clauses (supplement vs. substitution), (2) the referent of 'vacancies' (officers described previously), (3) the temporal references ('during the recess of the Senate' vs. recesses of state legislatures), and (4) other explicit constitutional provisions (e.g., Article I §3 clauses granting state executives power to fill Senate vacancies). Reading clauses in context prevents erroneous inferences such as granting the President power to fill Senate seats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty-making security via joint agency of President and supermajority Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary security against corruption in treaty-making is the combined agency of the Chief Magistrate and two thirds of a body (the Senate) selected by state legislatures; this joint action is intended as a pledge for fidelity in international negotiations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than relying on post-facto punishment of entire bodies, the Constitution secures fidelity by entrusting treaty power to a combination of actors whose numbers and characters reduce the risk of corrupt bargains. Attempts to punish large majorities of a deliberative body (e.g., two-thirds of the Senate) are impracticable and inconsistent with the immunity needed for free collective deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunity of members for collective acts and the necessity of trusting proper hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of legislative bodies should be exempt from punishment for acts done in their collective capacity; the society's security depends on entrusting deliberative power to proper hands and making it difficult for members to combine against public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom and independence of deliberation require that members not be punished for lawful collective decisions; protections thus rest on careful selection of representatives and institutional safeguards against collusion rather than retrospective punishment of majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral College design: combine popular input with deliberative electors and protections against tumult and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The election of the President should (a) allow the sense of the people to operate by having them choose electors for the special purpose, (b) use a small number of electors capable of deliberate judgment, and (c) minimize opportunities for tumult, disorder, cabal, intrigue, and foreign influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing electors (rather than a single national popular vote or an entrenched body) brings popular legitimation while enabling deliberation. Electors assembled and voting within their states, dispersed and transient, reduce the risk of sudden corruption or foreign tampering. The process also provides contingencies (House selection from top five if no majority) to secure a qualified chief magistrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and structure safeguards for electors and presidential independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors must be chosen so as to be free from undue bias: no senator, representative, or person holding a place of trust or profit under the United States may be an elector; the electors' transient existence and separation ensure independence of the President from other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding current officeholders from being electors diminishes partisan bias toward incumbents and reduces the potential for collusive influence. The special electing body and the method of re-election by such a body secure the President's independence from continual dependence on other branches or factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice-President chosen by same method with safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President is to be chosen in the same manner as the President, with the additional considerations that (a) the Vice-President should not be taken from the Senate (to preserve the Senator's regular vote), and (b) the Vice-President may need the same qualifications as the President because he may substitute for the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the Vice-President outside the Senate preserves the voting balance of the States in that body (so the President has only a casting vote). Choosing the Vice-President via the same electors ensures comparable deliberative and independence qualities for the person who might assume the chief magistracy.
